title: Metadata, Taxonomy, Ontology, and Folksonomy

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Metadata, Taxonomy, Ontology, and Folksonomy.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Metadata is data that describes content: author, date, status, topic, audience, location, relationship, and more. A taxonomy is a controlled classification system. An ontology adds more explicit definitions and relationships between concepts. A folksonomy emerges from user-created tags. Each balances control, flexibility, maintenance cost, and discoverability.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose structure proportionate to the task. Controlled fields make filtering and governance reliable; user tags can expose real language and emergent categories. A useful system documents definitions, owners, allowed values, and how changes are made. Without this, two teams can use the same label to mean different things and silently break retrieval.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Choose semantic machinery by the decisions it must support
turns.text: What changes when we look at choose semantic machinery by the decisions it must support?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Metadata records properties of an object. A taxonomy controls categories and their broader, narrower, or related structure. An ontology explicitly models entities, relationships, constraints, and sometimes inferential rules. A folksonomy captures participant-created tags.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: More structure can improve retrieval and interoperability, but also increases governance and the harm caused by a wrong definition.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Every value includes provenance, effective date, cardinality, missing-state semantics, permission, and owner. “Unknown” is never converted to “no.” Patient tags such as “quiet entrance” can expose useful language and future research needs, but do not become authoritative access claims. Automated enrichment remains a suggestion with confidence and review history.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The semantic model is tested with competency questions and edge cases. If it cannot answer “show step-free clinics whose access information was verified recently” without misleading omissions, either the data or the promise must change. lesson 134 brings this structure back to the evidence a person sees before choosing a route.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: research repository?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Free tags reveal how researchers describe studies, while controlled audience, method, consent, region, and date enable reliable reuse. Treating tags as authority creates synonym drift; forbidding them loses emergent language. A governed mapping preserves both functions.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at choose the semantic layer required?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Metadata describes an object through fields such as type, date, owner, audience, status, and rights. A taxonomy provides controlled categories and hierarchical or associative relationships. An ontology expresses richer entities, properties, and rules. A folksonomy captures participant-created tags and emergent language.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use the least complex layer that supports the decisions and retrieval required.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Define provenance, value constraints, cardinality, ownership, and lifecycle. Controlled structures improve consistency but require governance; user tags improve flexibility but create synonym, ambiguity, spam, and moderation needs. Map useful folksonomy terms into controlled concepts without erasing community language.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Test authoring burden and retrieval benefit. Missing or unreliable metadata can make facets and personalisation misleading. Automate suggestions where they remain reviewable, and audit drift, unused fields, category imbalance, and orphan concepts.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Semantics distribute power: categories determine what is visible, comparable, and reportable. Include affected perspectives when classification carries social or consequential meaning.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Govern semantic change as product change
turns.text: What changes when we look at govern semantic change as product change?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Vocabulary changes are tested against search, navigation, analytics, APIs, content, staff workflows, and historical records. Merging two clinic categories may simplify browsing but destroy a distinction required for referral routing. A folksonomy can reveal patient language and emerging concepts, yet it requires moderation and mapping before becoming authoritative domain data.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Metadata is an organisational agreement disguised as a technical field. If no one owns the vocabulary or update rules, a taxonomy becomes stale faster than the interface around it.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we look at more closely?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Model the information before implementing filters. Identify entities, attributes, relationships, valid values, hierarchy, lifecycle, source of truth, and permissions. Then decide which terms must be controlled for reliable retrieval and reporting, which can remain flexible, and how user language will be captured without corrupting the canonical structure.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Metadata quality directly affects search, navigation, recommendations, analytics, and AI retrieval.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Failure modes to watch

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Field without definition: teams enter the same metadata label with incompatible meanings. Taxonomy without owner: classifications become stale as content and services change. Filter illusion: an interface offers facets that the data cannot populate reliably. Folksonomy as authority: user tags are treated as a governed classification without review.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A library can list thousands of reports, but cannot reliably filter by topic, audience, region, or publication status because those attributes were never defined consistently. The interface problem begins long before the filter.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: lesson 132 showed the visible retrieval experience. lesson 133 explains the underlying meaning system. lesson 134 returns to the moment before someone chooses a route: information scent.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Pick a catalogue or content library. List three filters, infer the metadata each requires, and identify one ambiguous value that could make the filter untrustworthy.
